title: Text features | CatBoost
why_relevant: CatBoost is the strongest practical candidate for this competition because the dataset mixes numeric, categorical, and short free-text complaint fields.
extracted_technique: Use CatBoostClassifier with explicit `text_features`, plus controlled tokenizers/dictionaries/feature calcers so complaint text is converted into numeric features inside the model without separate TF-IDF code.
takeaway: CatBoost directly supports numerical, categorical, text, and embedding inputs, and its text processing works on CPU and GPU. That makes it the best anchor model for a shared local/Kaggle pipeline with minimal glue code.

title: LightGBM GPU Tutorial
why_relevant: LightGBM is a strong fallback or diversity model for structured features and dense/sparse text-derived features, especially if CatBoost text tuning stalls.
extracted_technique: Run LightGBM with explicit GPU device settings and multiclass objective for dense engineered features or a sparse TF-IDF branch.
takeaway: LightGBM GPU requires explicit device configuration and is best used as a controlled secondary pipeline, not necessarily the primary one. It remains useful for fast ablations and a sparse text fallback.

title: TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data
why_relevant: This dataset is medium-large tabular classification with 80k rows, so a large-data tabular foundation model is a legitimate high-capacity candidate rather than an academic curiosity.
extracted_technique: Use TabICL as a pretrained classification model for large tables, optionally with dense reduced complaint features appended to structured columns.
takeaway: TabICL is explicitly designed for large classification tables and reports strong performance versus CatBoost on bigger datasets. Given the repo already includes `tabicl`, it deserves a frozen shortlist slot, but only as an optional model because checkpoint/runtime stability still matters.

title: GitHub - soda-inria/tabicl
why_relevant: The GitHub repo gives the practical deployment details missing from the paper, including checkpoint versions and fit/predict expectations.
extracted_technique: Treat TabICL as a scikit-learn-like optional model, cache the checkpoint locally, and disable it cleanly if download or memory fails.
takeaway: The repo confirms usable checkpoints and practical large-table inference expectations. It also makes clear that TabICL should be integrated as a toggleable candidate, not a hard dependency for the first pass.

title: Machine-Learning-Based Electronic Triage More Accurately Differentiates Patients With Respect to Clinical Outcomes Compared With the Emergency Severity Index
why_relevant: This is primary clinical evidence that triage-time models benefit from combining vitals, chief complaint, and active medical history, which mirrors the competition schema closely.
extracted_technique: Build triage models from triage-time structured signals plus complaint/history features; use the model to better separate intermediate-acuity cases where humans are inconsistent.
query: site:pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov machine learning emergency triage chief complaint vital signs acuity
takeaway: The paper reports that an ML triage system built from vital signs, chief complaint, and active medical history improved or matched ESI and was especially useful for the crowded middle-acuity region. That strongly supports keeping complaint text and patient history in the competition pipeline.

title: Using Machine Learning To Augment Emergency Department Triage
why_relevant: This thesis directly argues that patient history and complaint text add value beyond basic triage fields and provides a realistic ED modeling blueprint.
extracted_technique: Merge triage data with prior utilization/history features and complaint-language representations; compare low-dimensional operational models with higher-capacity models.
query: "Enhancing emergency department triage with machine learning"
takeaway: The thesis argues that adding patient history materially improves triage-time prediction and that chief-complaint language should be standardized or embedded. That aligns well with the 1:1 `patient_history.csv` and `chief_complaints.csv` tables in this competition.

title: Categorical Data — xgboost documentation
why_relevant: XGBoost is the best dense-tree diversity model after CatBoost, especially if we append reduced text features and keep pandas categorical dtypes.
extracted_technique: Use `XGBClassifier(tree_method="hist", enable_categorical=True, device="cuda")` on a dataframe with categorical dtypes plus dense engineered text/SVD features.
takeaway: Modern XGBoost can natively consume categorical dataframe columns on GPU, which lowers preprocessing risk and makes it a practical second model beside CatBoost. The main caution is keeping category handling consistent and storing the model in JSON/UBJSON.
